Case Vignette: Marcus

Marcus is a 19-year-old man who lives with his mother and younger sister in a rented duplex on the outskirts of a mid-sized city. He works the evening shift at a fast-food chain, assembling burgers and working the fry station. He has been there for eight months, and while he is reliable, his manager has noticed he has become increasingly withdrawn and jumpy over the last several weeks.

The event that changed everything happened in early spring, during a night of severe storms. Marcus had just gotten home from his shift, around 11:30 PM. His mother and 14-year-old sister were already asleep. He was in his room, scrolling through his phone, when the tornado warning siren began to wail. He remembers the sound as something physical-a deep, mechanical howl that seemed to vibrate through the floorboards. He ran to wake his family. The power went out. The house began to shake, and then he heard a sound he cannot forget: a low, grinding roar, like a freight train passing directly through the living room.

He got his mother and sister into the interior hallway. He remembers pressing his back against the wall, his arms wrapped around his sister's head, his mother crouched beside them. He could feel the pressure change in his ears, a painful popping sensation. The windows in the front of the house blew inward, and the back door was ripped off its hinges. It lasted less than two minutes, but Marcus says he felt himself die in that hallway. He was certain the roof would go, that they would be pulled up into the blackness. He remembers thinking, very clearly, This is it. This is how we end.

They survived. The house was heavily damaged but structurally intact. The neighborhood was unrecognizable. Trees were snapped in half, cars were overturned, and the air was thick with dust and the smell of wet insulation. For the first few weeks afterward, Marcus felt strange-numb, but also hyper-alert. He helped his mother board up windows and sort through salvageable belongings. He told himself he was fine. Everyone was fine.

Now, eight months later, he is not fine.

Marcus cannot sleep through the night. He wakes up three or four times, usually around the same hours as the storm, his heart hammering, convinced he hears the siren or the wind. He has started checking the weather obsessively. Even a forecast for a thunderstorm sends a spike of adrenaline through his chest. He avoids going to the basement at work to retrieve supplies because the concrete stairs and the low ceiling remind him of the hallway. He has told no one this.

At work, he has become easily startled. Last week, a coworker dropped a metal tray behind him, and Marcus spun around, dropping the spatula, his hands shaking. The coworker laughed, but Marcus felt a hot wave of shame. He has started to feel detached from the customers, from the chatter in the kitchen. He goes through the motions-flipping patties, bagging fries-but he feels like he is watching himself from a distance. He has stopped hanging out with his two close friends. They want to go to a concert next month, but the idea of being in a loud, crowded space with no easy exit makes his stomach turn.

He has not told his mother how bad it is. She is still anxious herself, and he feels he has to be the strong one. He says he is just tired. He is tired. The effort of pretending to be okay, of pushing down the images of the shaking walls and the roar of the wind, is exhausting. He has started drinking a beer or two before bed to try to quiet his mind, but it does not help. He just wakes up more groggy.

Marcus does not know why he cannot just get over it. The storm is over. His family is safe. He tells himself he is being weak. But at night, lying in the dark, his body remembers what his mind tries to forget.
